column5: The Lagos Plan (OAU, 1980) opens with a Preamble that blames external forces and colonial and neo-colonial exploitation for Africa's condition but also says (para 17, food chapter) that member states 'have not usually accorded the necessary priority to agriculture'. Its figures: Africa's GDP about 2.7 per cent of world per capita income, average about 166 US dollars; continental growth no more than 4.8 per cent a year 1960 to 1980 (oil exporters 7 per cent, least developed 2.9 per cent); 20 of the 31 least developed countries; 97 per cent of world chrome reserves, 85 per cent of platinum, 64 per cent of manganese. It sets guidelines: resources for Africans, a shift from raw-material exports, self-reliance with outside help only 'to supplement' and an eventual African Common Market and Economic Community. The course's contrast 'Berg blamed domestic policy, Lagos stressed self-reliance' needs the nuance that Lagos itself admits domestic failings.

The plan's trade and finance chapter (paras 249 to 257) calls for preferential trade areas by 12/1984, removing obstacles to intra-African trade by 1990, state trading organisations and joint multinational production firms, control of foreign trade by 'national structures' (state or indigenous private), regulation of transnational corporations and transfer pricing, a payments union and an African monetary fund, a target of 2 per cent of world industrial production by 2000, and calls on industrialised countries and international institutions for 'increased financial assistance and aid'. It contains no call to repudiate debt. Policies such as state marketing and exchange controls are what the Berg Report criticised. Chapter VIII admits that member states fail to fund the institutions they create (paras 258 to 262).

I served the chapter blocks of the 37,599-word text in order. Book pp. 15 to 64 (industry to transport) were skipped as sector plans. The second half of the food chapter and the last third of the trade and finance block, and chapters VIII to XIII, were served but I examined only the trade and finance and institutions sections, so the review is partial.
